THE READING TRADITION AS A BASIS FOR MASORETIC NOTES

body.p: 1. The main contention of this paper is that the notes of the masorah are often based on the
reading tradition, that is, on the spoken form of the word in question, not on its written form.
This is most clearly shown by the use of the term רסח to describe words in which no vowel
letter is ever used, as1
Ps 138:2 /3imrät’ekä/ occurs 12 times and is not written with י .
Clearly the note provides information about the spelling of a particular spoken form. The term
רסח refers to the vowel segol, which is often written with yod before the kaf of the 2ms
suffix, but is never so spelled in this word. Many other examples occur, as

3. Masoretic notes are more often thought of as based on a written form or on a grammatical
form than on the spoken form. A survey shows that the spoken form is just as important a
basis for classification as these others. The above examples show words which have the same
spelling, but represent different grammatical forms and have different spoken forms, and so
are treated as different. Words may also be treated as different where different spoken forms
differ in spelling, but represent the same grammatical form, as

5. These illustrations do not represent a fixed practice, but they do show the importance of
the spoken form as a basis for categorization. Anyone used to reading masoretic notes will
be well aware that the spoken form is used in this way, but the fact is worth emphasis for two
body.head: E. J. REVELL
body.p: reasons. Biblical scholars tend to regard the stabilization of the reading tradition as the final
stage in the development of the masoretic text. This is no doubt true for some details, but the
extensive use of the spoken form as a basis for notes on spelling shows that the reading
tradition played a major part in the effort to maintain a stable text. The stabilization of the
reading tradition must, then, have occurred at an early period, as I have argued elsewhere2.
The second reason for emphasizing the importance of the spoken form as a basis for masoretic
notes is that this function is sometimes overlooked by masoretic scholars. The remainder of
the paper attempts to show how the concept may help to further the understanding of the
methods of the Masoretes, and so help to elucidate obscure notes.
6. Where a list in the MM covers the different spellings of a single spoken form, the notes
of the MP on the individual examples of that form may refer either to the spoken form or to
the written. Both are often used in such a way as to provide the fullest possible informa-
tion. E.g.

7. When organized in this way, the notes of the MP provide a maximum of information with
a minimum of writing. This method is used to the full in the description of the feminine plural
imperfect forms of the qal of אוב . These forms are spelled in four different ways, and
pronounced in two, and the pronounciation does not correlate fully with the spelling.
Moreover, the conjunction (in one of three possible pronounciations) may or may not be
prefixed to the form. The concordance of Even Shoshan lists these forms in seven different
categories.
8. The first example of a feminine plural imperfect qal form of אוב occurs in Gen 41:21.

It should be noted that this group of lists differs from the previous one in that it uses the terms
אלמ and דסח, not ביתכ. This suggests a different origin, or a different viewpoint. List [7]
is clearly based on the spoken form. It lists the two different spellings of the spoken form
/tebo3’ena/. The information it provides is thus different from that provided by any of the five
statements so far considered. List [6] appears to give the same information as list [3], but if
that was its intention, it is surprising that the yod, which is a concern of this list, is not
indicated in the spelling. The spelling of the form suggests that the list is the same as [4]. If
so, both references are wrong. A third possibility is that the spelling of the form, and the
reference to Esther, are as intended. If this is so, the purpose of the list is to describe the use
of waw in the spoken form /täb’onä/. The title should read
, and reference
should be made to the second form in Jer 9:16 (not the first), and to 2 Chr 9:21, as well as
to Esther. As in list [1], this list is based on the spoken form and refers to the spelling of
holem. Since the note is based on the spoken form, the yod in the form in Esth 4:4 is not
considered. It is easy to see how the presence of the Esther reference could lead to the
conclusion that the wrong form in Jer 9:16 had been referred to, leading to the «correction»
of the list to its present form.
11. If this reconstruction is correct, this pair of lists is not a garbled repetition of MM 1579,
as suggested by Weil and Cassuto. It deMs with the spelling of the two spoken forms which
represent the f.pl imperfect qal of אוב: /tebo^enä/ in list [7], and /täb’onä/ in list [6]. The
form of list [6] as reconstructed implies its corollary: that the remaining examples of /täb’onä/
have no vowel letter. Consequently this pair of lists gives complete information on the use of
vowel letters in the spoken realizations of the grammatical form.

body.head: E. J. REVELL
CONCLUSION
body.p: 15. If this reconstruction is correct, then, the MM and MP of L were designed to provide
complete information on the spelling of this confusing set of forms in abstract, complete
information on the use of waw to represent holemy and almost complete information on the
spelling of forms with a prefixed conjunction. Similar use of the MP to refer to the basic
information on spelling provided in the MM, but not to all the information, can also be seen
in the note on םיאישנ. MM 1367 (at Josh 22:14) gives a complete description of the spelling.
This must be considered to be based on the spoken form, as it includes examples conventional-
ly assigned to different words. The MP refers to the two basic categories of spelling, but (as
with the notes on the f. pl. imperfect qal forms of אוב) not to the catchall groups, nor to
unique spellings. Instead, it notes three cases where the word /nesi3’im/ is joined to a
preceding word with maqqef, forming a unique combination; it notes the variant spellings of
the two cases where /nesi3’im/ has both the article and the conjunction prefixed, and it notes
that in four cases the word represents the semantic field of «cloud». Taken together, the MM
and MP in such cases provide as much information as possible on the word in question. This
seems to me to represent a common practise, and so a further argument for the correctness
of my reconstruction of list [6], dealing with /täb’onä/. Whether or no that list did, in origin,
refer to the spoken form, however, it is clear that many masoretic notes are based on the
reading tradition, not on the written text. The understanding of this is important to the full
appreciation of the purpose and methods of the masoretes.
body.head: THE READING TRADITION AS A BASIS FOR MASORETIC NOTES
RESUMEN
body.p: En la nota de MP de Leningrado sobre ךתרןקא de Sal 138,2, bm ±י «doce veces,
y haser», la expresiön haser es superflua por lo que se refiere a la ortograffa, puesto que la
palabra nunca se escribe con mater lectionis. Debe de referirse a una vocal que pudiera estar
representada, aunque no lo est6, por una mater lectionis, es decir, al segol que define la forma
como pausal. Tales notas indican el importante papel desempenado en la transmisiön del texto
por la tradiciön de lectura, antes de la introducciön de los signos vocälicos. En este articulo
se dan ejemplos de otras notas que se comprenden mejor a partir de la forma hablada de la
palabra y se discuten casos en los que este concepto puede utilizarse para explicar notas que
aparecen confusas o inconsistentes.
body.head: SUMMARY
body.p: In the note in the MP of Leningrad on ךתר^א in Ps 138:2,
«twelve times,
and haser», the statement haser is superfluous as a reference to the spelling, as the word never
is spelled with a vowel letter. It must refer to a vowel which might be spelled with a vowel
letter, but is not, that is, to the segol which marks the form as pausal. Such notes indicate the
important part the reading tradition played in the transmission of the text before the
introduction of vowel signs. The paper gives examples of other notes which are best
understood as based on the spoken form of the word, and discusses cases where this concept
can be used to elucidate notes which appear confused or inconsistent.
